paras: The Anniston calaboose shooting was the killing of two Black men, named in the press only as Greenwood and Hammond, by the town marshal and his deputy at the lock-up in Anniston, Alabama, in late November or early December 1881. The officers fired when a crowd of Black men pressed them as they jailed a prisoner, and an inquest and a preliminary hearing cleared them. Newspapers across the country carried the story as a riot in 'a mining town' put down by police.

According to a local account reprinted in the Chicago Tribune, several hundred Black and white people gathered in Anniston on Saturdays, and on this Saturday there was 'more than the usual amount of drinking' among the Black visitors. About noon the marshal arrested a Black man for carrying concealed weapons, struck another with a club to keep the crowd back, and after a trial before Justice of the Peace H. L. Jeffers locked the prisoner in the calaboose.

Later the marshal arrested a second man, Hammond, and was followed to the calaboose by what the account called 'a howling, profane gang of negroes' urging the prisoner not to let himself be locked up. At the door the crowd pressed so closely that the marshal could not unlock it, and a white man named Mulke took the keys while the marshal drew his pistol and ordered the crowd back. In this version Greenwood, described as 'the leader of the rioters', then struck the marshal on the head with a rock, and the marshal shot him down.

At the same moment Deputy Marshal Smith fired on the crowd and hit Hammond, who ran up a flight of steps and fell. Four shots were fired; one man died at once and the other on the following Monday morning, and the order of the inquests suggests Hammond died first. The Decatur wire gave a shorter version in which 'many colored men' used 'stones and pistols' and the police, restoring order, 'shot and killed two negroes.'

Justice Jeffers held inquests over both bodies, and in Greenwood's case the jury found that he died at the hands of officers 'in the lawful discharge of their duty.' The wire reported that the policemen were 'arrested and exonerated,' and an Alabama news column in the Memphis Daily Appeal said they were discharged on preliminary trial. No report of any further proceedings appears in the coverage.

The Decatur dispatch ran on December 3 in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, the St. Paul Daily Globe, the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer, both Wheeling dailies and the Salt Lake Herald, under headings such as 'Riot in an Alabama Mining Town' and 'A Riot and Two Men Killed.' The telegraph garbled the town's name as 'Ansmith,' 'Annestoa' and 'Ausnisto,' and the Salt Lake Herald's printing credited the shooting to a single 'policeman.' The Lancaster paper called the dead men 'two of the rioters,' and later printings in Nevada and Memphis repeated the dispatch into the following week.

Only the Chicago Tribune carried the long local account, headed 'Two Negroes Killed by Officers of the Law' and credited to the 'Jacksonville (Ill.) Republican,' which told the story entirely from the officers' side. The Memphis Daily Appeal printed the discharge of the officers in its Alabama news on December 4 and again on December 17. All of the coverage came from white newspapers, and none gave Greenwood's or Hammond's full names or any account from Black witnesses.

The papers disagree on the date: the Decatur wire of December 2 said the riot happened 'yesterday,' and other printings said Thursday, Friday or Saturday. The local account placed it on a Saturday with a death the following Monday, which, since the Tribune printed it on December 4, means a Saturday no later than November 26.

accounts.label: Wire report (Decatur)
accounts.gist: A riot at Anniston in which many colored men used stones and pistols; the policemen, restoring order, shot and killed two negroes and were arrested and exonerated.

accounts.label: Local account (credited to the Jacksonville Republican)
accounts.gist: On a Saturday crowd day, Black men pressed the marshal and deputy as they took a second prisoner to the calaboose; after Greenwood hit the marshal with a rock, the marshal shot him and the deputy shot the prisoner Hammond; an inquest cleared the officers.

accounts.label: Alabama news column
accounts.gist: The officers who killed the two negroes while quelling the riot were discharged on preliminary trial.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the short Decatur dispatch under headings such as 'Riot in an Alabama Mining Town', 'An Alabama Riot' and 'A Riot and Two Men Killed', presenting the shooting as police restoring order.

The Chicago Tribune's reprinted local account, headed 'Two Negroes Killed by Officers of the Law', describes 'a howling, profane gang of negroes' and quotes the verdict that the officers acted in 'the lawful discharge of their duty'.

versions.value: 'yesterday' from a Decatur, Dec 2 dateline (Thursday, Dec 1)
'Last Saturday', second victim dying 'the following Monday morning'

conflicts.note: The local account is the most detailed and the only one with names and an inquest; because the Tribune printed it on Dec 4 and it reports a death on the Monday after the riot, its Saturday must be November 26 or earlier, before the Decatur wire's 'yesterday'. The wire's date may be the date the news reached Decatur; the evidence does not settle it.
